about: Semitone's style library: tags you combine (like Suno/Udio style tags) and the profiles behind them. A profile describes musical habits across many songs (chords, tempo, range, rhythm, sound, production), never any single song: no melodies, lyrics, recordings or MIDI are copied, and no voice is imitated. Each 'dna' point carries a confidence (high = sourced, med = some evidence, low = hunch) and sources, in the same shape as STYLE_DNA in web/semitone-studio.html. Wiring: see AGENTS.md, 'Style library and tags'.

tagKinds.label: Genre
tagKinds.help: Sets the core: chords, rhythm, structure.

tagKinds.label: Soundtrack & media
tagKinds.help: The vibe of a score, show, film or game.

tagKinds.label: Composer
tagKinds.help: A composer's writing habits (Orchestral, or Compose for small-ensemble writers).

tagKinds.label: Producer
tagKinds.help: How it's produced: drums, sounds, effects, arrangement tricks. Layers on top of any base.

tagKinds.label: Mood
tagKinds.help: Nudges key, tempo, density and brightness.

tagKinds.label: Era
tagKinds.help: Picks period instruments, drums and mix colour.

tagKinds.label: Your reference
tagKinds.help: A song or album you own, read by the song analyser: only numbers are kept (key, tempo, structure, energy, chords, tonal balance).

blendRules: The first base tag (genre, artist, soundtrack, composer or reference) sets the core profile.

Each further base tag blends in: chord transition weights (m) are averaged with weight 0.35, numbers (bpm, density, leap, register, swing) move 35% towards it, and its DNA points are listed under 'also from'.
A producer tag replaces the production layer (kit, groove, instruments, sound, articulation, mix moves) but never the chords or melody habits. Two producers: the second adds only its mix moves.
Mood, era and instrument tags apply small deltas (below) after blending, clamped to the engine's ranges.
Conflicts are shown, never silently resolved: e.g. Jazz + Trap asks whether the bass walks or plays 808s.
After choosing, a card lists what each tag changed, with Undo. The song is regenerated only when the user presses Use these tags.

accordion.label: Accordion
accordion.needs: a new accordion instrument (not in INSTR yet)

upright-bass.label: Upright bass
upright-bass.needs: a new upright bass instrument (bassgtr is the stand-in)

existingTags.about: The current styles and orchestral templates become tags too, so nothing is lost.

style.name: Camp synth-pop
style.desc: Big major IV–V–I–vi loops coloured with added 6ths and 9ths, 80s synths and drums, a theatrical voice that saves its top notes for the chorus.

art.info: Theatrical: accented phrase starts, held top notes with vibrato, short punchy notes in the verse.

arrangement.preChorus: hold the ii chord for the whole pre-chorus
arrangement.drumsTrick: double the beat-four snare every other bar (a Motown take on the backbeat)
extras: pedal steel as an unexpected colour

profiles.mixHint: Wide 80s synth stack, multi-tracked; bright and loud; strings and pedal steel tucked behind.

dna.intro: Chappell Roan's songs, produced and co-written by Dan Nigro, pair simple major-key loops with jazzy colours, 80s drums and synths, and a theatrical vocal.

points.t: Good Luck, Babe! loops IV–V–I–vi in D major, with an added 6th and 9th on the V and a 9th on the vi for jazzy colour.
The pre-chorus holds a single ii chord and the bridge stays on it too.
The tempo drifts between about 113 and 121 BPM, unusual for modern pop.
80s-sounding drums with a Motown-influenced backbeat (the beat-four snare doubled in alternate bars) and an 80s synth groove.
Verse melodies sit on chord tones with syncopation; chorus phrases open on the highest notes. The delivery is theatrical (Kate Bush and Tori Amos are cited).
Dan Nigro co-writes and produces; he describes building songs around the artist's voice and story.

style.name: Electro dance-pop
style.desc: Minor-key dance-pop at about 120 BPM: i–III–VII–iv and i–VI–VII loops, robotic verses, a chorus that opens up, stutter hooks.

art.info: Clipped, robotic verse lines and accented hooks; the chorus opens into longer notes.

arrangement.hooks: a vocal hook opens the song; a stuttering hook follows the chorus
arrangement.needs: a stutter-edit effect for the post-chorus hook (not in the engine yet)

profiles.mixHint: Clipped marching beat, soaring electronics, dry upfront vocal; synths carry over from section to section.

dna.tagline: minor-key electro dance-pop with stutter hooks
dna.intro: Lady Gaga's early hits with RedOne set dark minor loops at a dance tempo under 80s-inspired synths, with robotic verses and big, clear choruses.

points.t: Just Dance: C♯ minor, 119 BPM, C♯m–E–B–F♯m (i–III–VII–iv), uptempo dance-pop with electropop and synth-pop elements.
Poker Face: G♯ minor, 120 BPM, verse G♯m–E/G♯–F♯, chorus G♯m–E–B–F♯ (i–VI–III–VII), vocal range F♯3–B4.
80s-inspired synths and robotic verses; a vocal hook opens the song and a stuttering hook follows the chorus.
Critics heard clipped marching beats with soaring electronics and a mild R&B flavour.

style.name: 70s soft rock
style.desc: Few chords used three ways, a hypnotic steady groove, Rhodes and layered guitars, three-part harmonies on every chorus.

art.info: Relaxed, conversational lines; held notes lightly shaped, never belted.

arrangement.harmony: three-part harmony on the chorus, doubled
arrangement.sections: verse, pre-chorus and chorus can share the same chords; change texture instead (a tom accent into the pre-chorus, vibraphone with delay, congas at the back)
arrangement.drums: an 8-bar drum loop feel: steady and hypnotic

profiles.mixHint: Warm 70s tape; guitars spread across the stereo field; congas placed far back; bass simple and droning.

dna.tagline: warm 70s soft rock: few chords, hypnotic grooves, stacked harmonies
dna.intro: On Rumours, Fleetwood Mac built rich records from very few chords: Lindsey Buckingham changed texture, not harmony, to make sections feel different, over steady grooves and three-part harmonies.

points.t: Dreams began as 'just three chords'; Buckingham made three sections from identical chords that each sound different.
points.used: low chord variety; sections differ by texture

points.t: An eight-bar loop of Mick Fleetwood's drumming gave Dreams its deep, hypnotic effect; the bass is simple and softly droning.
points.used: steady groove, low ghost notes, rootfifth bass

points.t: Three-part harmonies were doubled for a fuller sound; the chorus harmonies came from Buckingham playing triads on piano.
Keyboards across Rumours: Fender Rhodes (the basis of Dreams), Hammond B3, Clavinet, Wurlitzer and grand piano.
Don't Stop uses a triplet snare rhythm into a shuffle; Never Going Back Again uses brushes.
Tempo around 115–125 BPM for the mid-tempo songs; ballads slower.

style.name: Funk rock
style.desc: Dorian minor riffs built from jams: a busy, melodic bass that knows when to lay out, clean bright guitar, half-rapped verses and sung choruses.

art.info: Rhythmic, half-rapped verse lines full of short notes and ghosted syllables; choruses sing out.

arrangement.bass: melodic and busy, but leaves space so the busy moments stand out (fewer notes, more impact)
arrangement.guitar: clean, raw Strat-into-amp tone; clear single lines and varied textures rather than distortion walls
arrangement.needs: a slap-bass articulation option (not in the engine yet)

profiles.mixHint: Raw, dry and close (recorded in a house); drums live and punchy; little processing.

dna.tagline: jam-born funk rock: melodic bass, clean guitar, rap-sung verses
dna.intro: On Blood Sugar Sex Magik, produced by Rick Rubin, the band moved from funk-metal toward melodic funk rock: Flea played fewer, more melodic notes and John Frusciante favoured clear lines over noise.

points.t: Flea cut back the slap technique for melodic bass lines and a minimalist approach: fewer notes so the busy moments stand out.
Frusciante's guitar was less noisy, leaving room for clearer lines and textures, over a raw, unprocessed Strat-and-Marshall tone.
Songs grew from jams; Give It Away came from one. Rick Rubin helped arrange drum beats, guitar melodies and lyrics.
Funk and rap rhythms in the verses, melodic sung choruses.
Riffs often sit in a minor key with a major IV (Dorian colour).

style.name: Parisian waltz
style.desc: Waltzes that turn like a merry-go-round: rippling piano arpeggios, an accordion tune, simple repeating patterns and small toy-like colours.

instr.lead: accordion (needs a new instrument; organ is the stand-in)

art.info: Light and clear: detached waltz notes, the odd grace note, no slides.

arrangement.accompaniment: a repeating piano figure (arpeggios or oom-pah-pah) that never stops
colours: a typewriter or hand-claps as percussion
arrangement.form: the main waltz returns in several versions (piano alone, accordion, full)

profiles.mixHint: Intimate and dry, like a small room; no drums; instruments panned as if around a table.

dna.tagline: merry-go-round waltzes for piano and accordion
dna.intro: Yann Tiersen's Amélie score is built from waltzes and simple repeating patterns, with the accordion giving it its French character and small colours (chimes, mandolin, a typewriter) adding charm.

points.t: The accordion is the most prominent instrument and gives the score its French character.
Waltzes are central: the main theme comes in three versions and waltzes recur, giving a merry-go-round effect.
The piano pieces use simple accompaniment patterns, arpeggios and rippling figures; one is described as Chopinesque.
Colour instruments include mandolins, celeste-like chimes, a music box, hand-claps, a typewriter and ondes Martenot.
Harmony mostly simple diatonic minor and major loops.

style.name: Analog synth score
style.desc: Warm analog synth arpeggios and pads, a slow pulse, dissonance used to build dread; few or no drums.

art.info: A synth lead: long tones and slow glides, no vocal-style ornaments.

arrangement.ostinato: an arpeggiated synth pattern runs through each cue
arrangement.build: layers enter one at a time; intense scenes 'go even harder'

profiles.mixHint: Warm and 70s-sounding rather than cold digital 80s; depth and slow movement, never harsh.

dna.intro: Kyle Dixon and Michael Stein of the band Survive scored Stranger Things on analog synths; the show was pitched to them as John Carpenter meets Italian giallo and Giorgio Moroder.
stats: John Carpenter, Goblin, Moroder, Tangerine Dream

points.t: Analog synths throughout; Stein's SH-101 is on nearly every record, plus kit-built modular gear.
The show's sound was pitched as John Carpenter, Italian giallo and Giorgio Moroder; Carpenter's use of dissonance to drive scenes is a cited influence.
They prefer warm, 70s-style recording to cold digital 80s sounds, aiming for depth and movement rather than harshness.
Arpeggiated synth patterns are a signature of the main theme.
Slow tempos, roughly 80–90 BPM for the main cues.

style.name: Swing jazz
style.desc: ii–V–I progressions with sevenths and extensions, a walking bass, swung eighths, a ride-cymbal groove and comping chords off the beat.

profiles.groove: swing (new: ride-cymbal pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, feathered kick)

instr.bass: upright bass (needs a new instrument; bassgtr is the stand-in)

art.info: Swung phrasing with scoops, falls and ghosted notes; accents on the off-beats.

profiles.form: 32-bar AABA (A = 8 bars) is the default; also 12-bar blues. Sections are named A, A, B (bridge), A, then solo choruses over the same form.
engineNeeds: a 'swing' groove (ride pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4)
chord extensions on every chord by default (7, 9, 13) and tritone substitution in the suggestion engine (SUGSTYLE tri already exists)
the AABA and 12-bar blues forms in the structure list
improvised solo choruses: a melody generator that varies the head over the form

Bossa nova.needs: a bossa groove and nylon-guitar comping pattern

profiles.mixHint: Small-room acoustic sound: piano centre, bass close, drums with lots of ride and brushes; little compression.

dna.tagline: swing: ii–V–I, walking bass, ride cymbal
dna.intro: Classic small-group jazz runs on ii–V–I progressions with seventh chords, a walking bass line on every beat, swung eighth notes and a ride-cymbal groove, usually in 32-bar AABA or 12-bar blues forms.

points.t: The ii–V–I is the most common progression in jazz standards.
Walking bass: one note per beat, chord tones on strong beats, passing tones leading to the next root.
Swing eighths are played long–short; the ride cymbal and the hi-hat on 2 and 4 keep time.
32-bar AABA and 12-bar blues are the standard forms.

dna.note: Jazz points are general music-theory knowledge rather than one artist's habits; add sources when the Classroom jazz lesson is written.

mixMoves: 16th-note tremolo on long synth pads, so held chords pulse
tape chorus-echo and spring reverb on keys
a wide room sound on drums and backing vocals
an arpeggiated synth bass carries the chorus low end
arrangement: layer a vintage sound with a modern one for contrast
build parts from processed sustained pads and arpeggios

dna.intro: Jack Antonoff (Bleachers; Taylor Swift, Lorde) builds records from 80s drum machines and synths, processed pads and arpeggios, and roomy stereo textures.

points.t: LinnDrum drum machine across early Bleachers work, for a driving Radio Ga Ga-style beat.
Roland Juno-6 as a favourite: its arpeggiated low end as the foundation of a chorus. Also Korg M1 presets and the Yamaha DX7 for an 80s character.
Soundtoys Tremolator on long synth pads to make 16th-note arpeggios; Roland RE-501 Chorus Echo for spring reverb.
Two room mics in the corners of his home studio for wide stereo room sound and backing vocals.

rules.glueHook: repeat a lyric phrase across sections
rules.syllableMatch: lyric syllables line up with melody notes
rules.contrast: strong contrast between verse, pre-chorus and chorus

arrangement: introduce one new element at a time
the strongest hook gets the most space without being overused
layer.aR: Raise the A&R check's weight on 'chorus before 0:50' and 'repetition of the hook'; feeds the prosody and rhyme tools.

dna.tagline: 'melodic math': fast choruses, matched syllables, glue hooks
dna.intro: Analyses of Max Martin's hits (the 'melodic math' idea, from researcher Asaf Peres; Martin himself may not use the term) point to fast routes to the chorus, syllables matched to melody, and repeated 'glue' hooks.

points.t: Most of his hits reach the first chorus before about 50 seconds.
Lyric syllables are matched to melody notes, and a 'glue hook' lyric repeats across sections.
One new musical element at a time; strong contrast between sections; melodies easy to memorise.

dna.note: These are songwriting rules, so this tag shapes structure and the A&R check more than sound.

mixMoves: vocal close and intimate, harmonies about as loud as the lead
a chopping tremolo (no smoothing) synced to 8ths or 16ths on a vocal or synth
reverb and delay printed into the parts
found sounds as percussion (household clicks, a drill, an audience)
arrangement: sparse: rhythm and layered harmonies matter more than a busy arrangement
upright piano as the writing instrument

dna.tagline: intimate bedroom pop: close vocals, found sounds, chopped effects
dna.intro: Finneas produced Billie Eilish's debut in his bedroom: a tight, quiet room for vocals, heavy vocal effects, non-musical found sounds and harmonies stacked as loud as the lead.

points.t: Vocals tracked in a small bedroom for a tight, intimate, quiet sound; harmonies often as loud as the lead.
A harsh tremolo at 0% smoothing, synced to 8ths or 16ths, to chop a signal; Logic's Vocal Transformer for a vocal effect.
Non-musical sound effects in the production (an oven, a dentist drill, audience reactions).
points.used: found-sound percussion (needs a small SFX sample set)

points.t: Writes on acoustic piano, records parts with virtual upright pianos; reverbs and delays printed before the mix.

mixMoves: big analog synth pads
a throbbing synth bass
an expressive synth solo with bends and glides, often over the outro
808 and tuning locked to the song's key
layer.harmony: minor keys with a brief lift to the relative major, then back to minor for melancholy
arrangement: add an outro section for a synth solo
leave gaps for an extra layer to fit in

dna.tagline: huge analog synths and expressive solos over hip-hop
dna.intro: Mike Dean (Kanye West, Travis Scott) is known for big analog synth pads, throbbing bass and expressive synth solos, on Moog, Oberheim, Jupiter-8 and Yamaha CS-80 synths.

points.t: Moog synths (Matriarch, Grandmother, Memorymoog, Minimoog), Roland Jupiter-8, Yamaha CS-80, Oberheim OB-X and Four Voice; he calls the CS-80 the most expressive synth.
His instrumentals feature a throbbing bassline, large synth pads and a synth solo over the top.
He uses minor keys with a brief move to the relative major, then back to minor for a melancholy feel; he insists the 808 and Auto-Tune match the key.

mixMoves: 80s-inspired synth stabs
a clipped, marching dance beat
a stuttering vocal hook after the chorus
a spoken or chanted vocal hook to open the song
arrangement: rock influences under dance-pop: big, simple, memorable

dna.intro: RedOne co-wrote and produced Lady Gaga's breakthrough hits; he calls himself 'a rock guy' and blends familiar sounds with a twist aimed at the moment.

points.t: Produced, programmed and played Just Dance (119 BPM) and Poker Face (120 BPM): synth-pop and dance-pop with 80s-inspired synths.
A vocal hook opens Poker Face and a stuttering hook follows the chorus.
Rock influences (Led Zeppelin, Deep Purple, Kansas, Foreigner); he blends familiar sounds with a current twist.

mixMoves: dry and upfront: little reverb, few effects
performance over polish: keep small timing pushes and pulls
arrangement: strip it back: offer to mute every part that isn't essential, section by section, as one undoable card ('reduce')
variant 'Def Jam': programmed drum-machine beats with live rock guitar
layer.suggests: A 'Reduce' button: Semitone proposes which parts to take out of each section and plays the stripped version; you keep what you like.

dna.tagline: the reducer: only what the song needs
dna.intro: Rick Rubin calls himself a 'reducer' rather than a producer: he strips a song down to see what is actually necessary, works by feel and taste, and aims for honest, intense performances (Run-DMC, Beastie Boys, Johnny Cash, Red Hot Chili Peppers).

points.t: Calls himself a 'reducer': gets the point across with the least information possible, stripping a track down to what is necessary.
Works by taste and feel rather than technical skill; his aim is the artist's best work, not a signature sound of his own.
points.used: why this layer changes arrangement more than sound

points.t: Encourages removing layers until only the most authentic performance remains (linked to his Johnny Cash records); early Def Jam records mixed drum-machine programming with live rock instruments.
On Blood Sugar Sex Magik he helped arrange drum beats, guitar melodies and lyrics; critics heard his 'cold precision' in the sound.

dna.note: Rubin is known for an approach rather than a fixed sound, so this tag mostly removes things and keeps performances natural.

mixMoves: vocal compressed twice in series with a vintage-style reverb
programmed drums layered with samples (extra kicks, snares, small clinks, cymbals) for size
parts nudged by hand so the groove pushes and pulls
arrangement: start on piano and voice, build to a full band (the piano-ballad-to-rock arc)
a section can switch from half-time to double-time drums
tempo may drift or push up a few BPM towards the end (uses the tempo curve)
colour layers: big stacked strings, Mellotron, Juno organ sounds
layer.suggests: A 'Build it up' card: proposes the ballad-to-rock arc across your sections (piano only → band → double-time last chorus).

dna.tagline: piano confessionals that build into rock
dna.intro: Dan Nigro (Olivia Rodrigo, Chappell Roan) builds songs that often start on piano and grow into full band rock, with programmed drums made human, layered strings and vintage keyboard colours.

points.t: Vampire grew from a half-time groove to double-time drums at about 132–135 BPM; the first verse was slowed by 1 BPM by hand.
The intro piano was re-recorded on a grand piano for more body; strings were stacked in about 100 tracks; Mellotron and Juno 60 organ sounds add colour.
Programmed drums layered with samples (kicks, snares, small clinks, extra cymbals) and nudged in the timeline for a human push and pull; live drums re-recorded later.
Vocal chain: EQ, two 1176-style compressors in series, a de-esser and a vintage-style reverb.
On Chappell Roan's Good Luck, Babe! he produced and co-wrote; the tempo drifts between about 113 and 121 BPM.
points.used: links to the Chappell Roan profile

template.name: Dark fantasy saga
template.mood: A cello-led theme over a driving string riff, minor and major traded back and forth, octave doublings that grow with every repeat.

sections.name: Riff
sections.lesson: A string riff states the rhythm that drives the whole cue. Trading C minor for C major (the parallel key) keeps you unsure whether the story is hopeful or doomed.
sections.roles: violins II and violas: riff (ostinato); cellos and basses: root; timpani: soft pulse

sections.name: Theme A
sections.lesson: The cello carries the theme: wide range and a dark sound. The harmony walks i–v–♭VII–iv before coming home. The second violins keep the riff going so the sections stay linked.
sections.roles: cellos: melody; violins II: riff; violas/horns: harmony; basses: bass

sections.name: Theme B
sections.lesson: Starting on ♭VI instead of i gives a sense of adventure. Big leaps (octaves) and turning the theme's shape upside down make it new.
sections.roles: violins I + cellos in octaves: melody; horns: counter; low brass: bass

sections.name: Climax
sections.lesson: The theme returns an octave higher with the full orchestra: Djawadi raises the melody by an octave on repeats to add drama.
sections.roles: violins I/II + cellos: melody in octaves; brass: harmony and hits; percussion: drive

sections.name: Coda
sections.lesson: Back to the riff alone, still swapping minor and major, ending on minor.

variants.Player-piano covers: A Westworld-style option: re-arrange the user's own song as a solo player piano or string quartet cover. Only the user's own songs, never other people's.

dna.tagline: cello themes, string riffs, minor/major tension
dna.intro: Ramin Djawadi's Game of Thrones theme switches between C minor and C major, uses a driving riff shared by the second violins, and puts the cello up front.

points.t: Opens on C minor for two bars, then C major (the parallel key); the A section moves i–v–♭VII–iv; the B section starts on ♭VI.
The cello was chosen as the main instrument for its range and dark sound (the show's creators banned pianos and flutes).
A riff drives the piece and the second violin shares it in later sections; contour inversions, octave leaps and raising the melody an octave on repeats are recurring devices.
Influences include Beethoven, Brahms, Tchaikovsky and 80s rock, especially Metallica.
Westworld's score features player-piano style covers of rock songs.
Tempo and exact meter of the main title not confirmed from a source; set as a starting point.

soundtrackLibrary.about: Media you can pick as a tag. Each maps to a profile, a blend of tags, or both; the user sees it as one tag. Add more by the same pattern; anything without a researched profile is a blend of existing tags and is labelled 'approximate'.

referenceTag.about: 'Use a song or album as the style'. Two routes: (1) the song analyser reads audio files the user owns, on their computer, and saves only numbers (key, mode, tempo, section lengths, energy curve, chord-change statistics, loudness and tonal balance) as a private profile named after the file; nothing from the recording itself is stored or shared. Several files (an album) are averaged. (2) Typing a title that isn't in the library: offer the closest tags (genre, mood, era, instrument) for the user to confirm; if the built-in assistant (AGENTS.md idea 24) is approved later, it can draft a profile for review.
